hypothesis: Texts that blend subjective opinions with factual statements (e.g., “It’s obvious that…”) often yield mixed judgments, increasing disagreement.
Mentions of multiple entities or topics in a single short passage (e.g., “I love X but Y is terrible”) cause difficulty in deciding the primary target or polarity, leading to disagreement.
Mentions of multiple entities or targets within the same sentence increase disagreement as annotators may differ on which entity the main sentiment or label applies to.
Texts containing mixed or ambivalent sentiment (both positive and negative cues) are more prone to annotator disagreement than texts with a clear single-valence sentiment.
Domain-specific jargon, slang, or culturally localized references that some annotators may not recognize lead to higher disagreement rates.
Texts expressing subjective opinions without explicit stance markers (“maybe,” “I guess,” “sort of”) make it harder to decide the correct label, promoting disagreement.
Questions or rhetorical statements (rather than declarative opinions) create uncertainty about the author’s stance, fostering disagreement.
Highly subjective statements (opinions, personal judgments, moral stances) result in more disagreement since annotators’ own perspectives influence the label.
Very short or fragmentary texts lacking sufficient context (e.g., single-word replies, sentence fragments) generate more disagreement because annotators must infer intent.
